title: TikTok pack 1 (21 originals, Bill)
_note: TikTok pack 1 (Showrunner + Studio, 2026-10-24). 21 original animal Shorts for TikTok only: 14 at 25-35 s and 7 single-topic deep dives at 61-75 s (Creator Rewards floor is 60 s; each deep dive is one animal told longer, not a compilation). Shorts v2 rules (research/38, research/39 section 6): animal named in the first 2 words, claim-first hook on a full-bleed photo at frame 0, a new picture every <=3 s, one Fork + one tink per video, Threat Level card as the running gag, loop line runs into the hook. 11 of 21 end on a spoken comment question just before the loop line (never in the first 3 s). Hooks from research/43. Photos: iNaturalist research-grade CC0/CC BY, captive=false, looked at one by one (live wild animals of the right species, no injuries, no dead animals). Facts web-checked 10/24; sources on each hook beat; uncertain numbers softened ('about', 'up to', 'may'). Voice: Bill (vidIQ premium). Hook 'sources' list the evidence; '_len' marks short/deep.

beats.say: Ironclad beetles can survive being run over by a car.
beats.loop_say: So if I could come back as anything,
beats.short_title: This Beetle Can Survive Being Run Over by a Car 🪲
beats.bonus: The diabolical ironclad beetle's wing cases lock together like jigsaw pieces.
beats.comment: What would you want to be uncrushable? 👇
sources: Rivera et al. 2020, Nature (Purdue/UC Irvine): exoskeleton withstands ~149 N, about 39,000x body weight; the team ran one over with a Toyota Camry and it survived — https://edition.cnn.com/2020/10/21/world/beetle-engineering-intl-scli-scn
Interlocking elytra 'jigsaw' suture — https://www.ecowatch.com/diabolical-ironclad-beetle-science-2648439624.html
Diet: fungi under bark of dead trees (ironclad beetles, Zopheridae).

beats.say: Scientists tested one with a Toyota Camry. It survived.
Its shell can take about thirty-nine thousand times its own weight.
I fall apart if you look at me with a fork.
Threat to meatballs: none. It eats fungus.
Bombardier beetles fire a boiling chemical spray out of their rear end.
beats.loop_say: And that's the bug that won't stay eaten, because
beats.short_title: Bombardier Beetles Fire Boiling Spray From Their Butts 💥
beats.bonus: The spray reaches about 100 °C, boiling-water hot.
beats.comment: Would you pick one up? 👇
sources: Science News / Discover on Sugiura & Sato 2018: spray reaches about 100 °C — https://www.discovermagazine.com/bombardier-beetles-refuse-to-be-toad-snacks-37445

Sugiura & Sato 2018, Biology Letters: Pheropsophus jessoensis fed to Japanese toads; 43% of toads vomited the beetles 12-107 min later; all vomited beetles alive and active — https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.ng788
Smithsonian, 'How Exploding Beetles Can Survive Being Eaten Alive' — https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/how-exploding-beetles-cause-japanese-toads-vomit-180968095/
Mechanism: two chemicals (hydroquinones + hydrogen peroxide) mixed with enzymes in a reaction chamber in the abdomen.

beats.say: Two chemicals mix in a chamber inside its abdomen, and pop.
The spray hits about a hundred degrees Celsius. Boiling water.
I also come with a hot sauce. Nobody's scared of mine.
Now the weird part. In Japan, scientists fed these beetles to toads.
The toads swallowed them. Then the beetles fired, inside the toad.
Forty-three percent of the toads threw the beetles back up.
Some beetles were in there for almost two hours. Every one that came out was alive.
Swallowed whole, and it still won. I'd like to know how.
Threat to meatballs: low. Threat to toads: very high.
Would you pick one up? Comment.
Pufferfish poison is rated over a thousand times deadlier than cyanide.
beats.loop_say: And I'm the one people order on purpose.
beats.short_title: Pufferfish Poison Is Deadlier Than Cyanide 🐡
beats.bonus: Tetrodotoxin blocks the sodium channels nerves use to fire.
beats.comment: Would you ever try fugu? 👇
sources: Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety: tetrodotoxin over 1,000 times more toxic to humans than cyanide (some authorities); heat-stable, cooking doesn't destroy it — https://cfs.gov.hk/english/multimedia/multimedia_pub/multimedia_pub_fsf_178_02.html
Tetrodotoxin review (no antidote; blocks voltage-gated sodium channels) — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3942760/
Arothron diet: algae, molluscs, crabs, coral (genus accounts).

beats.say: Cooking doesn't destroy it, and there's no antidote.
Yet people pay extra to eat it. I'm perfectly safe. No one's impressed.
Threat to meatballs: low. It eats crabs and coral.
Would you eat it? Comment.
Horned lizards squirt blood out of their eyes. On purpose.
beats.loop_say: So if you ever see one crying,
beats.short_title: Horned Lizards Squirt Blood From Their Eyes 🦎
beats.bonus: The blood tastes foul to dogs, foxes and coyotes, but birds don't seem to mind it.
beats.comment: Did you know lizards could do this? 👇
sources: Live Science, short-horned lizard (squirts blood from its eyes) — https://livescience.com/animals/lizards/short-horned-lizard-the-inflatable-horny-toad-that-squirts-toxic-blood-from-its-eyes

A-Z Animals summary of studies: Texas horned lizard squirts up to about 5 ft (often 1-2 ft); restricts blood flow from the head until vessels near the eyelids rupture; foul to canids; doesn't deter birds — https://a-z-animals.com/articles/blood-shot-eyes-natures-most-gruesome-defense-mechanism/
Middendorf & Sherbrooke / 2005 Southwestern Naturalist (USDA): coyotes showed startle and avoidance; head-shaking — https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/icwdm_usdanwrc/511
Bad taste thought to come from compounds in their harvester-ant diet (worded 'likely').

beats.say: They're often called horned toads. They're not toads. They're lizards.
The squirt can reach up to about five feet.
It traps blood in its head until the pressure bursts tiny vessels near the eyelids.
Here's the trick. The blood tastes awful to dogs, foxes and coyotes.
In tests, coyotes shook their heads and backed off.
Birds don't seem to mind it. So against hawks, it just puffs up and looks spiky.
The bad taste likely comes from its diet. Venomous harvester ants.
If a coyote bites me, the only thing I squirt is gravy.
Threat to meatballs: none. It eats ants. I checked twice.
Stonefish are the most venomous fish known, and they look like rocks.
beats.loop_say: So before your next beach walk, remember,
beats.short_title: Stonefish Are the Most Venomous Fish, and They Look Like Rocks 🪨
beats.bonus: First aid: get out of the water, soak in hot water (about 40-45 °C), get to hospital.
beats.comment: Would you have spotted it? 👇
sources: Australian Museum, Reef Stonefish: 'the most venomous fish in the world'; thirteen dorsal spines deliver the toxin; most stings are on feet on reef flats — https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/reef-stonefish-synanceia-verrucosa-bloch-schneider-1801/
MedlinePlus / UF Health, stonefish sting first aid: hot water 40-45 °C, emergency care — https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002854.htm

beats.say: Thirteen spines on its back carry venom.
Most people get stung by stepping on one.
First aid is hot water, then the hospital.
It just sits there looking like nothing. Like me, on a plate.
Would you walk barefoot there? Comment.
Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat.
beats.loop_say: So if a moray smiles at you, remember,
beats.short_title: Moray Eels Have a Second Set of Jaws 🦷
beats.bonus: Mehta & Wainwright, Nature 2007: the first vertebrate known to use a second set of jaws to grab and move prey.
beats.comment: Which movie does this remind you of? 👇
sources: Mehta & Wainwright 2007, Nature 449:79-82, 'Raptorial jaws in the throat help moray eels swallow large prey' — https://fishlab.ucdavis.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/397/2020/05/Mehta-Wainwright-2007b.pdf
National Geographic, 'Moray eels attack with second pair of Alien-style jaws' — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/moray-eels-attack-with-second-pair-of-alien-style-jaws

beats.say: After the first bite, the throat jaws shoot forward, grab the prey, and pull it in.
Scientists filmed it in two thousand seven. Very sci-fi.
Two sets of jaws. I have zero. This feels unfair.
Threat to meatballs: high. It eats fish, crabs and octopus.
Sea cucumbers breathe through their butts.
beats.loop_say: And I thought my life was weird, but
beats.short_title: Sea Cucumbers Breathe Through Their Butts 🥒
beats.bonus: Pearlfish live inside some sea cucumbers, slipping in through the rear.
beats.comment: Would you touch one? 👇
sources: PBS NOVA, 'Sea Cucumber Butts' (breathing through the anus into respiratory trees; anal teeth) — https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/nature/sea-cucumber-butts.html
National Geographic, 'How this fish survives in a sea cucumber's bum' (pearlfish; evisceration) — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/how-this-fish-survives-in-a-sea-cucumbers-bum
Ucluelet Aquarium: organs expelled as defense, sticky; regrow (sources vary: days to weeks, worded 'over the next few weeks') — https://uclueletaquarium.org/?p=2094
Diet: they swallow sediment and digest the organic matter in it.

beats.say: They pull water in through the rear, into organs called respiratory trees.
And when something attacks, some of them shoot their guts out.
Sticky threads, or actual organs. The attacker gets tangled up.
Then it regrows them, over the next few weeks.
If I lose my insides, I'm not regrowing them. I'm a sandwich.
It gets worse. A fish called the pearlfish lives inside some sea cucumbers.
It wiggles in through the back door, and hides there.
Some sea cucumbers have tiny teeth back there, maybe to keep fish out.
Threat to meatballs: none. It eats sand. Still, no.
Would you touch one? Comment.
Praying mantises can catch hummingbirds.
beats.loop_say: So the next time you see a mantis waiting,
beats.short_title: Praying Mantises Can Catch Hummingbirds 🦗
beats.bonus: Most cases were in the US, where mantises wait at feeders and hummingbird flowers.
beats.comment: Would you still keep a hummingbird feeder? 👇
sources: Nyffeler et al. 2017, Wilson Journal of Ornithology 129(2): 147 cases of mantids catching small birds in 13 countries; ruby-throated hummingbird most often caught; >70% of cases in the US, often at feeders — https://conservation.unibas.ch/team/nyffeler/pdf/nyffeler2017wjo.pdf
Scientific American, 'Praying Mantises Catch and Eat Birds Alive' — https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/artful-amoeba/praying-mantises-catch-and-eat-birds-alive-video/

beats.say: Scientists found a hundred and forty-seven cases, in thirteen countries.
Most were in the US, often near hummingbird feeders.
A bug that eats birds. The food chain is clearly a suggestion.
Would you still keep a feeder? Comment.
Leeches got cleared by the FDA as a medical device.
beats.loop_say: And yes, that's a real prescription.
beats.short_title: Leeches Are an FDA-Cleared Medical Device 🩸
beats.bonus: Hirudin, from leech saliva, stops blood from clotting.
beats.comment: Would you let a doctor use one on you? 👇
sources: HealthDay, June 2004, 'It's Official: Leeches Are Medical Applications' (FDA clearance, Hirudo medicinalis, draining blood around skin grafts and reattached body parts) — https://www.healthday.com/health-news/alternative-medicine/it-s-official-leeches-are-medical-applications-519818.html
Pharmacy Times 2005 (three jaws with ~100 teeth each; hirudin anticoagulant) — https://www.pharmacytimes.com/view/2005-11-5004

beats.say: Their spit has hirudin, which stops blood from clotting.
Doctors use them to drain blood after skin grafts.
Medicinal leeches bite with three jaws, each with about a hundred teeth.
Three jaws. About three hundred teeth. And it's the one doctors trust.
Gila monsters chew their venom into you.
beats.loop_say: So remember, before it helped anyone,
beats.short_title: Gila Monsters Chew Their Venom Into You 🦎
beats.bonus: Exenatide (Byetta), approved in 2005, is a synthetic copy of exendin-4 from Gila monster venom.
beats.comment: Did you know a lizard helped make a diabetes drug? 👇
sources: National Park Service, Saguaro NP, Gila Monster (grooved lower teeth; the longer it hangs on and chews, the more venom; up to 35% of body weight in one meal; 3-4 spring meals) — https://www.nps.gov/sagu/learn/nature/gila-monster.htm
Smithsonian's National Zoo, Gila monster (may hold on more than ten minutes; up to a third of body weight per meal; fat in tail) — https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/gila-monster
Exenatide is synthetic exendin-4 from Heloderma suspectum venom; Byetta, first GLP-1 drug, FDA-approved 2005 — https://endeavors.unc.edu/fall2007/buse.php
'Only venomous lizard native to the US' (NPS) — cut from the script for length.

beats.say: No fangs. The venom runs up grooves in its lower teeth while it hangs on.
The longer it chews, the more venom gets in. It can hold on for over ten minutes.
It can eat about a third of its body weight in one meal.
A third. In one sitting. I'd be a starter.
Then it can go months without eating, living on fat stored in its tail.
Now the plot twist. Scientists found a hormone in its venom called exendin four.
A copy of it became Byetta, a diabetes drug approved in two thousand five.
It was the first of the drug family that now includes Ozempic.
Threat to meatballs: medium. Helpfulness: surprisingly high.
House flies can't chew, so they throw up on your food.
beats.loop_say: So the next time one lands on your sandwich,
beats.short_title: House Flies Throw Up on Your Food 🪰
beats.bonus: Their mouthparts are a soft sponge; they can't bite.
beats.comment: Do you still eat it after a fly lands? 👇
sources: ScienceAlert / The Conversation, 'Do flies really throw up on your food?' (regurgitate digestive juices onto solid food, then sponge it up; taste receptors on the feet) — https://www.sciencealert.com/do-flies-really-throw-up-on-your-food-when-they-land-on-it
HowStuffWorks, Housefly Diet (sponging mouthparts) — https://science.howstuffworks.com/environmental/life/zoology/insects-arachnids/housefly3.htm

beats.say: The juices turn it to liquid, then they mop it up with a spongy mouth.
They taste with their feet, so they know it's food the moment they land.
Lunch was on the counter for one minute. I need a moment.
Still going to eat it? Comment.
Dung beetles of one species can pull over a thousand times their weight.
beats.loop_say: So when you think you're having a hard day,
beats.short_title: This Dung Beetle Pulls 1,141 Times Its Own Weight 💪
beats.bonus: Male bull-headed dung beetles use their horns to fight rivals inside tunnels.
beats.comment: What's the heaviest thing you've ever pulled? 👇
sources: Knell & Simmons 2010 (Proc. R. Soc. B), Onthophagus taurus males pull 1,141x body weight, 'like a person pulling six double-decker buses' (summarised on Wikipedia, Dung beetle) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dung_beetle

beats.say: That's like you pulling six full double-decker buses.
The males use those horns to shove rivals out of tunnels.
They live on poop and they're thriving. I'm stressed.
Threat to meatballs: none. It only eats poop.
Turkey vultures throw up on anything that scares them.
beats.loop_say: So if you're planning to sneak up on one, know this.
beats.short_title: Turkey Vultures Throw Up on Anything That Scares Them 🤮
beats.bonus: Their strong stomach acid helps them eat carrion that could carry anthrax or botulism.
beats.comment: Would you get close to one? 👇
sources: Live Science, 'Turkey vulture: the bird that vomits acid up to 10 feet' — https://livescience.com/animals/birds/turkey-vulture-the-bird-that-vomits-acid-up-to-10-feet-and-poops-antiseptic-onto-its-legs

Walking Mountains Science Center, 'Why do vultures self-defense vomit?' (lightens them for take-off; acid neutralizes pathogens like anthrax and botulism) — https://walkingmountains.org/curious-nature/international-vulture-awareness-day/

Blumstein et al. 2017, Journal of Wildlife Diseases short communication: urohidrosis likely cools; the germ-killing claim is untested; vultures locate food mainly by smell — https://blumsteinlab.eeb.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/104/2017/05/Blumstein_etal_2017_JWD.pdf
Smell range: 'over a mile' (Center of the West) — worded 'sometimes over a mile'.

beats.say: The vomit is acidic, half-digested, and it can fly up to about ten feet.
Throwing up also makes them lighter, so they can take off faster.
Their stomach acid is strong enough to kill a lot of the germs in rotting meat.
Things like anthrax and botulism. They eat dead animals, and rarely get sick.
I've been left out overnight. I would like to not be found.
And they find that food by smell, sometimes from over a mile away.
On hot days, they pee on their own legs. It probably cools them down.
Threat to meatballs: high, if I'm left out.
Would you get close to one? Comment.
Giant water bugs inject spit that turns their prey into soup.
beats.loop_say: So if your toe feels a pinch in the pond,
beats.short_title: Giant Water Bugs Turn Their Prey Into Soup 🥣
beats.bonus: Some giant water bug fathers carry the eggs on their backs until they hatch.
beats.comment: Would you swim in a pond with these? 👇
sources: Belostomatidae (Wikipedia): proteolytic saliva injected through the beak, liquefied prey sucked out; 'toe-biters'; bite among the most painful but no lasting medical effects — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belostomatidae
Live Science, Lethocerus eating a fish from the inside out — https://www.livescience.com/38574-giant-water-bug-eats-fish.html

beats.say: Then they suck it out. Small fish, tadpoles, even frogs.
People call them toe-biters. Painful, but not dangerous.
Turning food into soup. That's my nightmare, and my recipe.
Would you swim with these? Comment.
Skunks can hit you with spray from about ten feet away.
beats.loop_say: So if one stomps at you, back off, because
beats.short_title: Skunks Can Hit You From 10 Feet Away 🦨
beats.bonus: A National Zoo biologist says skunks can hit a target up to 20 feet away.
beats.comment: Have you ever been sprayed? 👇
sources: Smithsonian, 'Ask Smithsonian: What Makes Skunk Spray Smell So Terrible?' (thiols, as added to natural gas; accurate up to 20 ft; refilling glands can take up to 10 days) — https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/ask-smithsonian-what-makes-skunk-spray-smell-so-terrible-180955553/
A few sprays per full charge (about 5-6; sources vary 5-8) — Northern Woodlands — https://northernwoodlands.org/outside_story/article/seasons-greeting-from-your-neighborhood-skunk

beats.say: The smell comes from thiols, the same kind of chemical added to gas.
It only has a few sprays. A refill can take ten days.
I also smell strong when threatened. Of garlic.
Bullet ants have the most painful insect sting ever ranked.
beats.loop_say: And I still think the worst part is that
beats.short_title: Bullet Ants Have the Most Painful Sting Ever Ranked 🐜
beats.bonus: Bullet ant pain can come in waves for up to 24 hours.
beats.comment: Would you wear the glove? 👇
sources: Britannica, bullet ant (name from the sting feeling like a gunshot; 4+ on Schmidt's index) — https://www.britannica.com/animal/bullet-insect

Schmidt's description: 'like walking over flaming charcoal with a 3-inch nail embedded in your heel'; pain for up to 24 hours; poneratoxin acts on sodium channels — https://www.sciencealert.com/?p=32967
Sateré-Mawé initiation with bullet-ant gloves (Brazil) — https://whyevolutionistrue.com/2014/08/06/the-worst-pain-known-to-humans-the-bullet-ant-gloves-of-brazil
Diet: nectar and small arthropods.

beats.say: It's named that because getting stung feels like being shot.
The pain comes in waves, and can last up to a full day.
Scientist Justin Schmidt rated it four plus, the top of his pain scale.
He compared it to walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel.
The culprit is a toxin called poneratoxin. It keeps nerves firing.
In Brazil, Sateré-Mawé boys wear gloves of these ants as a coming-of-age rite.
They do it on purpose. I panic when someone picks up a toothpick.
Threat to meatballs: low. It mostly eats nectar and small insects.
Would you wear the glove? Comment.
Woodpecker tongues wrap around the back of their skulls.
beats.loop_say: And when it's done eating, guess where it goes.
beats.short_title: A Woodpecker's Tongue Wraps Around Its Skull 🐦
beats.bonus: The tongue sits on the hyoid, a set of bones and cartilage that loops over the head.
beats.comment: What animal should Meatball explain next? 👇
sources: American Bird Conservancy, 'The Amazing Secrets of Woodpecker Tongues' — https://abcbirds.org/blog21/woodpecker-tongues/
TalkOrigins, Anatomy of the woodpecker's tongue (hyoid horns wrap around the skull) — https://poc3.talkorigins.org/faqs/woodpecker/woodpecker.html
Red-bellied woodpecker tongue nearly three times the length of its beak — https://www.todayifoundout.com/?p=2834 (popular source; worded 'almost')

beats.say: The tongue rides on long bones that loop over the top of the head.
A red-bellied woodpecker's tongue is almost three times as long as its beak.
That tongue could reach anything. I'm keeping my distance.
What animal should I do next? Comment.
Shrikes stab their food onto thorns and barbed wire.
beats.loop_say: So if you see a grasshopper on a fence,
beats.short_title: This Songbird Hangs Its Food on Barbed Wire 🐦
beats.bonus: Loggerhead shrikes are songbirds with a hooked, hawk-like beak.
beats.comment: Have you ever seen one of these pantries? 👇
sources: The Nature Conservancy, 'Shrikes: Meet the Bird That Impales Prey on Spikes' — https://blog.nature.org/2020/01/27/shrikes-meet-the-bird-that-impales-prey-on-spikes/

Yosef & Whitman 1992 (Evolutionary Ecology): loggerhead shrikes wait about 1-2 days before eating impaled toxic lubber grasshoppers; also Travis Audubon — https://travisaudubon.org/murmurations/bird-of-the-week (worded 'may wait')

beats.say: Shrikes are songbirds that hunt like hawks.
The spike holds the meal, or saves it for later.
With toxic lubber grasshoppers, they may wait a day or two, until the poison fades.
Skewered and left out for later. That's a kebab. I know kebabs.
Tarantula hawks are wasps that hunt tarantulas.
beats.loop_say: So if a tarantula ever looks nervous, it's because
beats.short_title: Tarantula Hawks Are Wasps That Hunt Tarantulas 🕷️
beats.bonus: Adult tarantula hawks mostly drink nectar from flowers like milkweed.
beats.comment: Have you ever seen one of these wasps? 👇
sources: Wikipedia, Tarantula hawk (female paralyzes a tarantula, drags it to a burrow, lays one egg; larva feeds on the living spider; sting among the most painful, pain lasting about five minutes; Schmidt's advice to lie down and scream; adults feed on nectar) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarantula_hawk
Newsweek coverage of a Pepsis paralysing a tarantula — https://www.newsweek.com/horrifying-video-shows-giant-wasp-paralyze-tarantula-so-living-spider-body-can-716711
Size up to about 5 cm (2 in) for the largest Pepsis.

beats.say: They're up to about two inches long, with bright orange wings.
The female stings a tarantula, and paralyzes it.
She drags it into a burrow and lays one egg on it.
When the larva hatches, it eats the spider. Alive. Saving the vital parts for last.
That's not a meal. That's a hostage situation.
For people, the sting ranks among the most painful in the world.
One scientist's advice if you're stung: lie down and scream.
The good news: the worst pain only lasts about five minutes.
And the adults mostly drink nectar from flowers.
Threat to meatballs: low. Threat to tarantulas: absolute.
Sea lampreys drink fish blood through a mouth full of teeth.
beats.loop_say: So if a fish has a round scar, now you know.
beats.short_title: Sea Lampreys Drink Fish Blood 🩸
beats.bonus: A sea lamprey can kill up to 40 pounds of fish during its feeding stage.
beats.comment: Would you swim in a lake with these? 👇
sources: Great Lakes Fishery Commission (sealamprey.org): sucking disc of sharp teeth around a rasping tongue; one lamprey can kill up to 40 lb of fish; largely unchanged for 340 million years — https://sealamprey.org/
CBC, GLFC's Marc Gaden: 'they bore a hole through the side of the fish, feeding on the fish's blood and body fluids' — https://www.cbc.ca/lite/story/1.4343218

beats.say: In the Great Lakes, one can kill up to forty pounds of fish.
Their family is older than the dinosaurs, by over a hundred million years.
No jaws. No bones. Still scary. I have no bones, and I'm brunch.
Would you swim with these? Comment.
Velvet ants aren't ants. They're wingless wasps.
beats.loop_say: So if you see a fuzzy red ant, remember,
beats.short_title: Velvet Ants Aren't Ants. They're Wasps 🐜
beats.bonus: Velvet ants aren't aggressive; females sting only in defense.
beats.comment: Have you ever seen a cow killer? 👇
sources: Wikipedia, Velvet ant (Mutillidae: wingless females, winged males; Dasymutilla occidentalis nicknamed 'cow killer', an exaggeration) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant
UW-Milwaukee Field Station, Velvet Ant — https://uwm.edu/field-station/bug-of-the-week/velvet-ant/

beats.say: This one is nicknamed the cow killer, for its sting.
It can't actually kill a cow. The name is an exaggeration.
Only females sting. The males have wings, and no sting.
Bright red, fuzzy, and called cow killer. I'm called Meatball.
